walkthroughs.body_html:
Inorganic Chemistry — a core area of GCSE Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Inorganic Chemistry brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Inorganic Chemistry.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: How is a dynamic equilibrium different from a static one?
options: A dynamic equilibrium means the system is still changing visibly.
In a dynamic equilibrium, forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates; in a static equilibrium, nothing is happening at the particle level.
Dynamic and static equilibria are the same thing because both show constant macroscopic properties.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH 0.

mcqs.q: What state are the ions in when defining lattice enthalpy of formation?
options: The ions start as solid elements before being assembled into the lattice.
Gaseous ions — lattice enthalpy is the energy change when one mole of solid ionic compound forms from its constituent ions in the GAS phase.
A dynamic equilibrium means the system is still changing visibly.
The ions are in aqueous solution before forming the lattice.

mcqs.q: When an acid neutralises an alkali, what is the pH of the resulting solution?
options: Approximately 7 if equivalent amounts of strong acid and strong alkali react — but it varies with strength.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH 0.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH exactly 7 regardless of the acid and base used.
The ions start as solid elements before being assembled into the lattice.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Combustion of alkanes”?
options: Compound containing only hydrogen and carbon.
Mixture of hydrocarbons (mostly alkanes), separated by fractional distillation.
Complete: alkane + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. Incomplete: produces CO and soot.
Saturated hydrocarbon with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — all single bonds.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Saturated”?
options: Compound containing only hydrogen and carbon.
Contains only single C–C bonds; cannot add more atoms across a bond.
Complete: alkane + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. Incomplete: produces CO and soot.
Saturated hydrocarbon with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — all single bonds.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Alkane”?
options: Methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀.
Contains only single C–C bonds; cannot add more atoms across a bond.
Saturated hydrocarbon with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — all single bonds.
Mixture of hydrocarbons (mostly alkanes), separated by fractional distillation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Crude oil”?
options: Complete: alkane + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. Incomplete: produces CO and soot.
Compound containing only hydrogen and carbon.
Methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀.
Mixture of hydrocarbons (mostly alkanes), separated by fractional distillation.
